• Common names: Whisker coral or Daisy coral
  • Minimum tank size: 15 gallons (~60 litres)
  • Keeping: easy; propagation: moderate
  • Lighting: low to medium; water flow: moderate
  • Optimal salinity: SG 1.023–1.025
  • Optimal KH: 8–12
  • Nitrate: 5–10 ppm
  • Feeding: photosynthetic / requires supplemental feeding
  • Tank placement: bottom to middle
  • Growth rate: moderate to fast
  • Temper: peaceful; not toxic; not invasive
  • Colour: purple, pink, green or blue-grey tentacles

When shopping, look for healthy specimens with good colouration, a robust body and fully extended polyps. Duncans with drab or faded colour, a slime coating or retracted polyps might not survive in your reef tank.

Duncan corals are highly sought after and many offline and online marine aquarium stores carry them. Obtain specimens from reputable dealers who keep captive-bred stock and use safe propagation methods.

Quarantine new corals and dip them to remove potential pests. Examples: Seachem Reef Dip, Blue Ocean Corals Coral Rx Dip Aquarium Treatment, Brightwell Aquatics Koral MD – Coral and Frag Dip Cleaner.

Duncan coral is an LPS coral whose origin can be traced to the Indo-Pacific, Australia precisely. It belongs to the genus Duncanopsammia and is a monotypic taxon, the only species of this genus.

It looks a bit like a button polyp, but button polyps lack the fleshy tentacles and calcified skeleton of Duncanopsammia, although their oral discs look the same.

Taxonomy: Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Cnidaria, Class Anthozoa, Order Scleractinia, Family Dendrophylliidae, Genus Duncanopsammia, Species Duncanopsammia axifuga.

Duncan coral is indigenous to Australia. It dwells on sandy and rocky seabeds in Australia and the South China Sea.

These corals are predominantly found in waters over 20 metres deep, affixed to a solid substrate but in areas where soft sand is abundant. There, they grow in colonies of clustered or branching individuals at the lower levels.

The species has a calcified skeletal structure and a wide striped, teal oral disc. Seemingly long fleshy tentacles form around the edges of the disc, usually purple/pink, green or blue-grey. It can grow in a compact/clustered form or branch out into individual fleshy heads attached to long, tubular collarites.

The recommended tank size is a minimum of 15 gallons (~60 litres). Duncan coral grows fast and produces new heads with ease. Small tanks are often not ideal, while larger tanks can hold a massive colony and allow proper spacing.

Duncan corals are hardy and relatively easy to keep. Perform partial water changes of 20–25% monthly or 10–15% every two weeks to keep the water clean and replenish trace elements. Test the water routinely to keep parameters in range.

Feed at least 2–3 times a week to encourage growth. Target feeding helps ensure the coral ingests the food quickly before tankmates snatch it.

Monitor your Duncans and other inhabitants closely. Move an unhealthy coral to a separate or hospital tank for treatment until it heals. An exposed coral skeleton often hints at excessive lighting or flow, so cut back on these; if it remains so after you correct the conditions, it may be a sign of death, and you should try to salvage the remaining colony.

Common problems

  • Brown jelly: a brown jelly-like goo, which can be caused by poor water quality, tissue damage, overfeeding, etc. It can spread rapidly to the whole colony or other corals if untreated. Solution: frag the head off, brush and siphon off any visible jelly, use iodine dips and move the coral to a hospital tank. The coral should be dipped in a freshwater dip (15 ppt) or iodine solution; broad-spectrum antibiotics can also cure the infection. Afterwards keep the coral in a quarantine tank to recover fully before returning it to the main tank. Do not overdose Lugol's solution; follow the bottle's instructions for your tank size.
  • Bleaching: usually a response to environmental stress such as direct lighting or changes in salinity, pH, etc. In a study, Duncan corals bleached under elevated temperature (32°C) and high light intensity; temperature and light act synergistically. The coral loses colour and turns pale or translucent as the symbiotic algae are expelled. Find the cause and fix it.
  • Not opening (retracting): many aquarists report Duncans staying closed for days or even weeks. Do not panic: it is normally sprouting a new head or just sulking. Sometimes they take a few months to settle in, seem not to grow, and then suddenly grow like crazy. Their flesh is sensitive, so if something keeps pecking at it (a foxface, blue tang, yellow tang or flame angel), the coral will retract to protect itself.
  • Abandoning the base (bailing out): uncommon, but sometimes heads leave the old skeleton. The real reasons are unknown; the reef community assumes it is due to swings in water parameters, which can stress the coral and stop calcification, causing polyps to detach. Test water parameters regularly at the same time of day.

• Temperature: 24–27°C
  • pH: 8.1–8.4
  • Hardness: 8–12 dKH
  • Specific gravity: 1.023–1.025
  • Calcium: 400–450 ppm
  • Magnesium: 1250–1,350 ppm
  • Strontium: 8–10 ppm
  • Phosphate: < 0.05 ppm
  • Ammonia: 0 ppm
  • Nitrate: 5–10 ppm

Do not lower nitrates too far, as it negatively affects these corals.

Lighting: Medium lighting is vital for healthy growth. They thrive in low to medium light, whereas high lighting may stress them. Avoid direct metal halides, which bleach and damage the tissue. Use full-spectrum LED lights or T5s; light output around 75–100 PAR is suitable. Duncan corals generally change colour depending on the lighting, whether white or blue light.

Flow: They cannot handle very strong flow, so provide moderate flow. It should be enough to bring suspended prey or food closer to the tentacles and prevent detritus from settling on the body. Excessive flow can harm the coral or make its polyps retract fully, hindering feeding. When flow is strong the tentacles are usually short and blunt; with less flow they are long and stringy.

Information online about lighting and flow conflicts: some keepers report success with strong flow and high light, others with low flow and medium light. This shows the coral is hardy, but the general consensus of the reef community is that moderate flow and medium light are optimal.

Placement: Duncan corals do not encrust onto the plug. Mount them in cooler spots, preferably in the low to middle sections of the aquarium, where they get the medium light needed for photosynthesis. Placing them on the sand is not recommended, as they are easily irritated if sand reaches them. Orientation (straight up, midway or horizontal) seems not to matter; a large colony often grows into a ball with some heads facing up, some horizontal and some downwards.

Most members of Dendrophylliidae are azooxanthellate (lacking symbiotic zooxanthellae) and rely on capturing food with their tentacles; Duncan coral is an exception. It receives nourishment through the photosynthetic activity of the symbiotic algae in its tissue. In addition, it uses its tentacles to capture plankton from the water column and pushes it to the mouth at the centre of the oral disc.

It benefits from regular supplemental feeding of small meaty foods and pellets, including:

  • krill
  • plankton
  • copepods
  • calanus
  • Reef Roids
  • cyclops
  • daphnia
  • mysis
  • finely chopped pieces of shellfish
  • vitamin-enriched brine shrimp
  • specialised pellet food

Do not just add these foods to the tank and expect the coral to catch them. Use a turkey baster or sea squirt feeder to squirt food directly onto the polyps; the coral quickly expands its tentacles to draw the meal in.

Frozen foods should be thawed and rinsed to make them easier to consume. Rinse chopped food several times to remove as much phosphate as possible.

Manual feeding should be 2–3 times a week, though the coral gets most of its nutrients from photosynthesis. Supplemental feeding boosts the growth rate. Do not overfeed: they are voracious eaters with very sticky tentacles and a strong feeding response. Some keepers reported their Duncan corals catching and eating Asterina starfish.

Duncan coral is prized for its peaceful nature and can coexist with other non-aggressive LPS corals and invertebrates.

Its tentacles remain extended day and night and retract when disturbed, for example when a curious fish nips at the polyps or aggressive tankmates move close. Polyps may also retract to avoid severe damage from excessive lighting or very high flow.

Maintain adequate spacing between Duncan corals and other inhabitants such as corals, sponges and anemones that possess powerful defensive mechanisms. Duncans may not hurt them, but they might harm your Duncans.

Unlike many other corals (Torch, Hammer, Frogspawn, etc.) that develop long sweeper tentacles to sting nearby corals in the battle for space, Duncan coral has none, so it cannot injure tankmates. Give it plenty of room to grow, since it forms many new polyps over time. Spacing also helps it avoid contact with tankmates.

These corals reproduce asexually by budding new individual polyps from mature (parent) polyps to form new colonies. One head can bud off as many as five within a couple of months. Alternatively, a healthy coral can be fragged to establish a new colony, ideally with a band saw.

During fragging, keep the corals wet at all times in a small bucket of water taken directly from their home aquarium; this water can also be used to rinse flesh from cuts.

  1. You need a decent-sized Duncan coral with a few heads.
  2. Take out the coral and irritate it slightly so that it retracts its tentacles.
  3. Using an electric bandsaw, divide the coral into several parts by cutting between polyps, cutting branches off as far below the polyp as possible. Do not use cutters or a scalpel: the skeleton is very dense. It is relatively easy to break by hitting it, but this is not recommended because the pieces will be uneven.
  4. After cutting, treat the new frags in an iodine solution to disinfect the cuts, which has been shown to greatly increase frag survival.
  5. Attach them to a frag plug using cyanoacrylate gel and place them in the reef tank.

Tip: soak the frag plug in water for a couple of minutes to release air bubbles from the ceramic. Tip 2: treat new frags with an iodine solution (for example Lugol's solution) to prevent disease, then attach them to live rock before placing them back in the tank.

Duncan coral is a popular, hardy and attractive large polyp stony coral, an excellent addition to established reef aquaria. Placed in the lower to middle sections of the tank, it adds a splash of vibrant green and purple. It can thrive in reef tanks with low or medium lighting and flow. Some reef keepers have left it unattended for several weeks without problems; although that is not good practice, it shows how hardy and forgiving the species is.
